title: Ethics in IT
subtitle: Climb the money ladder — one question per grade level

questions.q: Kant's categorical imperative requires that an ethical action must be justifiable as what?
options: A universal law that anyone in the same situation could follow
An action that produces the greatest happiness for the most people
A rule endorsed by a recognized professional code
A decision validated by a majority of stakeholders
questions.note: Kant's categorical imperative states: act only according to principles you could will to become universal laws. If an action cannot be universalized without contradiction, it is unethical.

questions.q: The utilitarian ethical framework judges the morality of an action primarily by which criterion?
options: Adherence to a formal code of professional conduct
The intrinsic rightness of the act regardless of consequences
The good character of the person performing the action
The greatest good for the greatest number of people affected
questions.note: Utilitarianism, associated with Bentham and Mill, evaluates actions by their outcomes. An action is ethical if it produces the greatest good for the greatest number of people affected.

questions.q: The principle of 'informed consent' in IT ethics requires that users:
options: Agree to terms of service in any format the company chooses
Receive comprehensible disclosure of what data is collected, how it will be used, and who it will be shared with -- before agreeing
Accept monitoring by employers as a condition of employment
Have access to all data collected about them at any time
questions.note: Genuine informed consent requires comprehensible, prior disclosure of data practices -- not terms buried in dense legalese. The user must understand what they are agreeing to before they agree.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a 'morally wrong but legally permissible' scenario in the IT context?
options: Hacking into a competitor's servers with management approval
Violating a software license agreement
Collecting user data through consent buried in a long terms-of-service document
Sharing personally identifiable information without a privacy policy
questions.note: Consent buried in a long ToS may be legally valid but is ethically problematic because it exploits asymmetric information. This is a classic example of the gap between legal compliance and ethical conduct.

questions.q: A social media platform removes posts it deems 'misinformation' about public health topics. Critics argue this restricts free expression. Which argument best defends the platform's right to act?
options: The platform is a public utility and must carry all speech
The First Amendment gives individuals an absolute right to speak on any platform
Private companies are legally permitted to set community standards and moderate content
Removing content is only justified if a court orders it
questions.note: The First Amendment restricts government censorship, not private actors. Social media platforms, as private companies, are legally permitted to set community standards and moderate content. Whether this is wise policy is a separate ethical debate.

questions.q: A developer uses a short snippet of GNU GPL-licensed open-source code in a commercial product but does not release the product's source code. What ethical and legal issue does this create?
options: A GPL license violation -- GPL code requires any derivative work to also be released under the GPL
No issue -- using a small snippet falls under fair use
A DMCA violation -- the developer copied digital content without permission
A trademark violation -- the GPL brand is being used without authorization
questions.note: The GPL is a copyleft license: it requires that any derivative work incorporating GPL code must also be released under the GPL. Distributing a proprietary product with GPL code without source disclosure is both a license violation and an ethical breach of open-source community trust.

questions.q: A hospital's IT team is migrating patient records to a cloud vendor. Which action is ethically and legally required before the migration under HIPAA?
options: Publishing a notice in a local newspaper informing patients of the move
Encrypting all records before uploading
Executing a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with the cloud vendor
Obtaining written consent from every patient whose record will be migrated
questions.note: HIPAA requires covered entities to execute a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with any vendor who handles Protected Health Information (PHI). Without a BAA, the hospital is legally exposed and ethically responsible for the vendor's data handling practices.

questions.q: The concept of 'software liability' in IT ethics concerns which ongoing debate?
options: Whether developers should be licensed by the government
Whether the software industry should be held to the same product liability standards as manufacturers of physical goods
Whether open-source software should be taxed like commercial software
Whether software patents should be abolished
questions.note: Software liability asks whether the software industry should face the same accountability as physical product manufacturers. Currently, EULAs routinely disclaim all warranties. Critics argue this creates a race to the bottom on software quality and safety.

questions.q: A team builds a predictive hiring algorithm with 85% overall accuracy, but it rejects candidates from historically underrepresented groups at twice the rate of other groups. The ethically correct response is:
options: Halt deployment, audit the training data and model for disparate impact, and retrain before release
Deploy the model because 85% accuracy is commercially acceptable
Add a manual review step only for rejected candidates in the affected groups
Disclose the disparity in the product documentation and proceed with deployment
questions.note: Disparate impact -- where a neutral-seeming system produces unequal outcomes for protected groups -- is a recognized form of discrimination. An 85% accuracy rate that systematically disadvantages a protected group is not ethically acceptable. The training data and model must be audited and corrected before release.

questions.q: Artificial intelligence tools used in criminal sentencing have been criticized for producing racially biased risk scores. The primary ethical objection is:
options: AI systems are too expensive for most courts to operate fairly
AI should only be used by federal courts, not state courts
Judges should not rely on any statistical tool in sentencing decisions
Defendants have a right to understand and challenge the basis for decisions affecting their liberty; an opaque score that may encode racial bias violates due process
questions.note: The core objection is accountability and due process: defendants have a right to understand and challenge the basis for decisions that affect their liberty. A black-box score that may encode racial bias and cannot be inspected violates fundamental principles of fair justice.

questions.q: The concept of technoethics argues that technology is:
options: Neutral -- only the intent of the user determines the ethical character of a technology
Inherently harmful and should be regulated by default
Shaped exclusively by market forces, not ethical reasoning
Not neutral -- design decisions encode values, and ethical reasoning must be integrated throughout the technology development lifecycle
questions.note: Technoethics holds that technology is not neutral -- design decisions encode values, and those values have real consequences. Ethical reasoning must be integrated throughout the lifecycle of technology development, not applied retroactively after harm occurs.
